items.readable_text:
Content:
Suppose that we are given a sector of a circle of radius [MATH: 4\,\textrm{cm},] like the one in the diagram below, where [MATH: m\angle AOB = \dfrac{\pi}4] radians. How can we find the length of the arc [MATH: \overset{\frown}{AB}?]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/a0ab710433a62119878410343df1ceee]

Content:
Let the length of the arc [MATH: \overset{\frown}{AB}] be denoted by [MATH: s.] To find [MATH: s,] we can use the arc length formula stated below:

Content:
[MATH: s = r \cdot \theta,]

Content:
where [MATH: r] is the radius of the circle and [MATH: \theta] is the central angle. Note that for this formula to work, [MATH: \theta] must be in radians.

Content:
In our example, we have [MATH: r = 4] and [MATH: \theta = \dfrac{\pi}{4}.] So, the arc length is given by

Content:
[MATH: s|= 4 ⋅ (π)/(4) = πcm.]

Content:
Note: To see where the arc length formula comes from, the trick is to set up a proportion.

Content:
The ratio of the arc length [MATH: s] to the circumference [MATH: C] must be equal to the ratio of the angle [MATH: \theta] to a full revolution of [MATH: 2\pi] radians. So, we have

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{s}{C} = \dfrac{\theta}{2\pi}.]

Content:
Substituting [MATH: C = 2\pi r] and making [MATH: s] the subject of the equation, we get

Content:
[MATH: (s)/(2πr)|= (θ)/(2π); 2π × (s)/(2πr)|= 2π × (θ)/(2π); (s)/(r)|= θ; s|= rθ.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Here, the length of the arc is [MATH: s = 6\,\textrm{cm}] and the radius is [MATH: r = 5\,\textrm{cm}.]

Rearranging the arc length formula, we have

[MATH: s|= r ⋅ θ; θ|= (s)/(r).]

Therefore,

[MATH: \theta = \dfrac{s}{r} = \dfrac{6}{5} \, \text{rad}.]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/a0ab710433a62119878410343df1ceee]

Content:
Let the length of the arc [MATH: \overset{\frown}{AB}] be denoted by [MATH: s.] To find [MATH: s,] we can use the arc length formula stated below:

Content:
[MATH: s = r \cdot \theta,]

Content:
where [MATH: r] is the radius of the circle and [MATH: \theta] is the central angle. Note that for this formula to work, [MATH: \theta] must be in radians.

Content:
In our example, we have [MATH: r = 4] and [MATH: \theta = \dfrac{\pi}{4}.] So, the arc length is given by

Content:
[MATH: s|= 4 ⋅ (π)/(4) = πcm.]

Content:
Note: To see where the arc length formula comes from, the trick is to set up a proportion.

Content:
The ratio of the arc length [MATH: s] to the circumference [MATH: C] must be equal to the ratio of the angle [MATH: \theta] to a full revolution of [MATH: 2\pi] radians. So, we have

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{s}{C} = \dfrac{\theta}{2\pi}.]

Content:
Substituting [MATH: C = 2\pi r] and making [MATH: s] the subject of the equation, we get
